JobTitle1: Principal Engineer and Head of DevRel
Title: Your Agent's Tools Are a Dependency, Not a Prompt
Abstract: Most tool-calling setups treat a tool definition as text injected into a prompt, versioned nowhere and tested by nobody. This talk argues for packaging agent tool definitions as ordinary, importable Python: versioned, pip-installable, unit-tested, and pinned in CI like any other library your agent's sandbox depends on. When the tool definition and the sandbox's actual implementation drift, the agent calls a function that no longer matches its schema, and it fails in ways that look like model error but are really packaging error. I'll walk through a concrete pattern: tool functions as a versioned package, schema generation from real type hints instead of hand-maintained JSON, and CI gates that fail the build the moment a tool's signature changes without a version bump. This talk applies two decades of Python packaging discipline to the one part of agent infrastructure everyone still treats as a prompt-engineering afterthought.

Title: Prompting Is Not the System: Engineering Context, Contracts and Reliable Agent Behavior
Abstract: A prompt can influence a model, but it cannot replace an engineering system. When an agent has access to project context, tools, memory, and production workflows, reliability depends on the contracts around the prompt as much as on the wording inside it.  This talk moves from prompt-centric thinking to context engineering. We will examine a realistic agent workflow and identify where it breaks: incomplete or stale context, instructions that conflict with tool permissions, unstructured model output, retries that repeat side effects, and prompts that grow until nobody understands what the agent is actually allowed to do.  The session presents a practical model for reliable agent behavior:  - treat context as an explicit, versioned input contract; - separate stable policies, task context, retrieved knowledge, and user intent; - define tool schemas, permissions, validation, and failure behavior outside the prompt; - use structured outputs and deterministic handlers for decisions that must be predictable; - let the model reason where ambiguity exists, but keep high-risk actions behind policies and checkpoints; - evaluate complete workflows instead of judging isolated answers; - observe, test, and recover from failures in production.  Using AgentsKit as a concrete example, we will compare a prompt-only implementation with a bounded workflow that combines deterministic logic and model reasoning. The goal is not to eliminate prompts, but to put them in their proper place: one layer in a larger system of context, contracts, tools, evaluation, and operational feedback.  Attendees will leave with a practical checklist for diagnosing whether an agent needs a better prompt, better context, a stronger tool contract, or a different system design altogether.

Title: Prompting Is Not the Product: Designing Agent Instructions That Survive Production
Abstract: Most prompt-engineering advice stops at making a model sound smarter. Enterprise systems fail elsewhere: instructions conflict, context becomes stale, tools expand the blast radius, and nobody can explain why an agent acted.  This talk reframes prompting as part of systems architecture. Richard shares a practical method for designing agent instructions that remain reliable when connected to business data, workflows and APIs: define the job boundary, separate policy from task context, make tool permissions explicit, build verification into the workflow, and test the failure paths before release.  Attendees will gain a reusable blueprint for moving from clever prompts to production-grade agent behaviour—more dependable outcomes, clearer audits and safer autonomy.

Title: Whose gate is it?
Abstract: Every team running coding agents already has all three. A charter that says what the repository is about, a harness that decides how a turn happens, and a factory that decides how work ships. Almost nobody has drawn the lines between them, so a new rule lands wherever the person who noticed the problem happened to have commit access. Platform ships a harness and finds one team's opinion inside it. Development writes a charter and spends a third of it trying to configure a pipeline it cannot reach.  So I will put the levers on screen, context by context, and then walk a single rule down the six rungs where a gate can physically sit. Two more rungs sit off that chain, and both stay off it for a reason. On the way down, the context changes under you three times, and so does the team that owns the file.  Then the part platform engineers came for. There are two boundary lines here, and most designs only draw one. The context line asks what a thing governs. The ownership line asks who gets paged when it is wrong. Both lines agree at the charter, which belongs to development, and both agree at the factory, which belongs to platform. They cross inside the harness, which is where your org-design arguments have been living all along. You leave with that split named component by component, and with the rule that makes shared ownership survivable.

Title: Stop prompting. Start harnessing: how I run AI agents that don’t fall over
Abstract: Most demos show an agent completing one happy path. Real work is messier: long tasks, bad tool calls, context that overflows, and “it worked yesterday” failures.  I’ll walk through the harness I use when working with AI agents day to day: tools and memory, human checkpoints, catching loops before they burn tokens, and what I measure so I know the agent is actually helping.  You’ll leave with a concrete checklist for coding agents or product agents, plus failure modes I keep hitting so you don’t have to discover them live. No product pitch — practitioner patterns only.

Title: The AI Was the Easy Part: Making LLM Document Workflows Reliable Enough for Zero-Touch Automation
Abstract: Getting an LLM to read a legal document is easy. Making its output reliable enough for software to act on it without someone checking every result is much harder. At AVRillo, a UK conveyancing firm, I built a production workflow that receives property information by email, processes legal documents, performs external checks, raises enquiries, and opens a case automatically. The document-processing layer uses a multi-provider AI service spanning OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, and open-source models.  The interesting part was the weeks of iteration on real Land Registry documents needed before the output could be trusted inside a live workflow. In this talk, I’ll walk through what we learned about designing LLM-powered document workflows, dealing with unpredictable outputs and edge cases, separating the AI layer from deterministic business logic, and deciding when automation should stop and ask for human input.  Today, the standard path can run without human review, while exceptions pause for intervention rather than silently producing a bad downstream result. The talk is a practical look at the engineering around prompts and models that turns an AI demo into a production workflow.

JobTitle1: Technology Partner Aka Principal Solutions Architect
Title: Prompt Engineering for AI-Powered NEPA Compliance Automation
Abstract: Federal infrastructure, telecommunications, utility, and defense projects operating within historic districts and federally protected landmarks face complex environmental compliance requirements under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). Analysts must evaluate regulatory thresholds across multiple federal agencies, often relying on manual review processes that increase permitting timelines and administrative workload.  This session presents a real-world case study of building an AI-powered permitting intelligence platform that automates NEPA Categorical Exclusion (CE) determinations for historically sensitive sites. The talk focuses on the prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and system architecture patterns used to support regulatory decision workflows while maintaining traceability and human oversight.  The platform integrates large language models, computer vision, geospatial intelligence, and regulatory knowledge retrieval across federal and state data sources, including Google Street View, NPS IRMA, FCC ULS, EPA ECHO, USGS 3DEP, and State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) systems. Attendees will see how structured prompts, multi-step reasoning workflows, and evidence-grounded retrieval strategies are used to analyze construction drawings, GIS boundaries, LiDAR data, imagery, and environmental records to evaluate CE thresholds such as ground disturbance, structure height increases, right-of-way constraints, and potential impacts on National Register-listed properties.  The presentation will cover practical implementation lessons, including prompt design for regulatory reasoning, retrieval grounding techniques, multi-source evidence synthesis, documentation generation, auditability, and human-in-the-loop validation. It will also discuss architectural decisions, integration challenges, and workflow automation approaches that reduced environmental data retrieval time and streamlined coordination across multiple agencies.  Attendees will leave with reusable prompt engineering patterns and system design approaches that can be applied to other high-stakes domains where accuracy, explainability, compliance, and operational efficiency are critical.

Title: Prompt Engineering for Agentic Safety Assurance in Physical AI
Abstract: Physical AI systems in autonomous vehicles, robotics, and other safety-critical domains continue to adapt after deployment, placing pressure on traditional engineering workflows. MBSE provides a strong foundation for requirements, architecture, verification, and traceability, but recent AI-assisted tooling has focused mainly on model generation, requirement checks, and use-case discovery rather than continuous safety assurance.  This session introduces a prompt engineering approach for Agentic Systems Engineering, where bounded, human-supervised AI agents support compliance monitoring, requirements traceability, hazard coverage assessment, operational design domain validation, and safety-case integrity. The MBSE model remains the single source of truth, while carefully designed prompts, structured outputs, validation rules, and escalation paths guide agent behavior.  Attendees will learn how to design prompt templates for evidence retrieval, requirement-to-hazard mapping, compliance checks, and exception reporting across ISO 26262, ISO 21448, UL 4600, and ASPICE. The talk also covers practical risks, including hallucinated evidence, incomplete context, prompt drift, and over-automation, along with controls that preserve human accountability. The result is a practical architecture for using prompts and bounded agents to strengthen continuous engineering assurance for next-generation Physical AI platforms.

Title: Prompt Engineering for AML: Building Reliable Compliance Workflows at Scale
Abstract: Financial crime compliance workflows are increasingly incorporating large language models to summarize transactions, interpret investigation context, generate analyst narratives, and support regulatory reporting. Yet in AML environments, prompt engineering cannot be treated as simple instruction writing. Prompts must operate against governed data, produce traceable outputs, handle incomplete evidence, and avoid introducing unsupported conclusions into compliance decisions. This session presents a practical prompt-engineering framework for building reliable AI-assisted AML and Currency Transaction Reporting workflows on top of cloud-native data platforms.  Drawing on patterns from large-scale financial data modernization, the talk explores how structured prompts, retrieval context, schema-aware instructions, validation layers, and reusable prompt templates can connect curated transactional data with downstream compliance applications. It examines techniques for grounding responses in approved data products, separating factual extraction from interpretive reasoning, controlling output formats, and designing prompts that fail safely when evidence is insufficient. The session also covers testing, observability, prompt versioning, and audit logging for production environments. Attendees will leave with practical design patterns for turning prompt engineering into a governed engineering discipline that improves consistency, reduces manual effort, and supports defensible financial crime operations.

Title: Context Engineering Over Prompt Engineering: Building Stateful AI Agents in Production
Abstract: While basic prompt engineering helps generate simple completions, building robust AI agents capable of driving user behavior requires moving to full-scale Context Engineering. Drawing from real-world product experience scaling the AI Coach in Simple App (21M downloads), this session explores how to design, manage, and orchestrate complex context pipelines for LLM agents.  Max will contrast Agentic-centric versus Completion-centric architectures, demonstrating how state management, memory retrieval, and dynamic scenario routing yield far more reliable outcomes than static prompt tweaking. Attendees will learn practical techniques for managing personality and tone, establishing quantitative and qualitative evaluation frameworks (Evals), and rapidly testing new scenario paths without re-deploying core application logic

Title: Stuff It or Fetch It? Lessons from Building a Harness That Turns Podcast Transcripts into Content
Abstract: Your prompt is only a small part of what the model sees.  Every agent harness wraps your instructions in a system prompt, tool definitions, conversation history, and tool results before the model reads a word. Most of us never look at that assembled context, so when an output goes wrong, we blame the prompt.  This talk walks through building a minimal harness for a real job: turning interview transcripts from my podcast into newsletter drafts with pull quotes. Transcripts make a good test case because accuracy is checkable. A quote either appears in the transcript word for word or it doesn't, and it's either attributed to the right speaker or it isn't.  With the task and instructions held constant, I'll compare two ways of assembling context: stuffing the full transcript into the prompt, or giving the model tools to search and fetch what it needs. We'll look at quote accuracy, speaker attribution, and token cost for each approach, plus what broke along the way.  You'll leave with a clearer picture of what your harness actually sends the model, and a simple method for testing context strategies on your own data.

Title: From 150K to 22K Tokens: Context Engineering for MCP Tool-Calling
Abstract: MCP made it trivial to give an LLM hundreds of tools - and quietly catastrophic for your context window. Every pre-loaded tool schema is prompt real estate, and in our production setup, the model was burning 150K tokens "before reading the user's question". Worse than the cost: tool-selection accuracy collapsed under the noise, with the model picking the right tool only 42% of the time.  This talk covers Code Mode, a context engineering technique that replaces MCP's schema dump with typed API stubs the model reads like library code. Same tools, different presentation - and this presentation resulted in: 85% token reduction (150K to 22K), tool-selection accuracy up from 42% to 80%, and fewer round-trips per task.  I'll walk through how we measured the baseline (and why most teams never notice this problem), how typed stubs change what the model actually attends to, the failure modes we hit along the way - stub granularity, stale type signatures, when the model hallucinates methods that "should" exist - and when you should "not" use this pattern. You'll leave with a measurement approach you can run against your own agent the same day, and a simpler alternative if numbers are difficult to comprehend.  Everything shown is from a real production system, not a benchmark.

Title: Deciding What Goes in the Prompt: Knowledge Graphs for Privacy-Aware Context Assembly
Abstract: Context engineering usually focuses on relevance: retrieve the best chunks and fit them in the window. Privacy adds another question: is this data allowed in this prompt, for this user, for this purpose, in this region? Chunk-based retrieval has no way to answer that.  This talk shows how a privacy knowledge graph can govern context assembly. Drawing on experience building Records of Processing Activities (RoPA) pipelines and privacy infrastructure at Meta, plus retrieval and semantic search for GenAI products, Arpita walks through four techniques:  Modeling data sources, consent, processing purposes, and jurisdiction rules as a graph Filtering and redacting retrieved context based on graph queries before it reaches the model Using graph relationships to build structured, explainable context Tracing which data influenced a response  The talk also covers the latency and maintenance trade-offs of adding a graph to the context path.

Company1: MIO Partners Inc. | New York, NY
Title: Context Engineering for Agentic AI in Enterprise Knowledge Systems
Abstract: As organizations move beyond AI copilots and begin deploying agentic AI systems, many discover that model performance is only part of the challenge. The harder problem is ensuring that agents have access to trusted, governed, and contextually relevant information while operating across complex enterprise environments. This session shares practical lessons and architectural patterns for building enterprise knowledge systems that support reliable agent behavior at scale.  Drawing from real-world enterprise AI design challenges, the talk examines why traditional prompt engineering approaches, static Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, and conventional knowledge architectures often struggle in environments where information changes frequently and governance requirements are strict. Attendees will learn how context engineering helps address issues related to knowledge freshness, provenance, consistency, permissions, and operational reliability.  The session introduces Demand-Driven Context (DDC), a framework that uses agent interactions, execution outcomes, and failure patterns to identify the knowledge that has the greatest operational impact. Rather than relying exclusively on top-down knowledge modeling, DDC enables organizations to continuously refine context based on how agents and users actually work.  Attendees will also explore the evolution from traditional RAG implementations to AgenticRAG systems, where agents iteratively retrieve, evaluate, and synthesize information to complete tasks more effectively. The presentation discusses architectural decisions, governance controls, and implementation considerations for building compound AI systems using agent registries, task planners, knowledge services, and human-in-the-loop workflows.  The talk concludes with practical guidance for auditing enterprise knowledge infrastructure, establishing governance-first AI architectures, and improving collaboration between humans and intelligent agents. Participants will leave with actionable approaches for applying context engineering principles to prompt engineering and agent orchestration initiatives in production environments.

Title: Prompt Engineering Is Not Enough: How to Publish Products for Agents
Abstract: Most prompt engineering advice stops at the model boundary. In practice, the bigger leverage is often outside the prompt: the surfaces an agent can read, call, and trust. In this talk I will show how I made my own portfolio agent-ready with an MCP server, machine-readable resume APIs, llms.txt, AI-focused indexes, and a hiring flow that agents can complete without scraping a visual UI. The point is not novelty. It is reducing the cost of understanding and acting. I will connect prompt design, tool descriptions, structured outputs, and machine-readable product surfaces into one system, and show why teams that only optimize text prompts leave product capability on the table.

Title: What Running a front facing AI Agent Taught Us About Prompt Engineering
Abstract: Getting an AI agent to work in a demo is easy. Keeping it reliable once real customers are talking to it is a different problem. Real users ask things you never planned for, mix languages and tone, push the agent toward answers it shouldn't give, and occasionally have conversations that go wrong without anyone noticing.  In this talk, I share what we learned taking a customer-facing AI agent from pilot to production. We'll look at why a single large system prompt breaks down under real traffic, and how moving to a structured approach (intent detection, grounded tool calls, and clear handoff rules to humans) made the agent more predictable. I'll cover how we used real failures and escalations as our evaluation set, what we log on every conversation so prompt changes can be tied to actual outcomes, and the guardrails we added for topics where a wrong answer has a real cost.  Attendees will leave with a practical checklist for designing, testing, and monitoring prompts for any agent that talks directly to customers.

Title: From Prompt to Product: How I Used AI to Design, Build, Integrate, and Launch Real Apps
Abstract: Prompting is not the beginning of bringing your idea to life it starts long before your first prompt. This session will have attendees leaving with not just understanding the power of their prompt in development but also:  1.  How to create a repeatable process when building a product 2. Participants will understand how to go from novice prompt to expert 3. How to make sure your prompt keeps your product in scope and recognize when it hallucinates.  4. The attendees will leave with a sense of understanding how to use tools like Resend, OpenAi Realtime, APiIs, and other tools for integration and how they fit in the process.

Title: Detecting 70 Kinds of Bias with a Model You Own: Replacing LLM API Calls in a Real-Time News Pipeline
Abstract: Prompting a frontier LLM to flag bias in news works well in a demo. In production, with articles arriving continuously from publishers and social media, the cost, latency and inconsistency soon become a problem. This talk describes how we built a system that classifies around 70 types of bias (from framing and omission to loaded language and ideological slant) and rewrites stories to be balanced. We began with LLM prompts, used their outputs plus human review to build a large, politically balanced dataset of news stories, and trained an in-house model that replaced most of the API calls.  You'll see how we designed the taxonomy, how we kept the dataset balanced, where prompting still beats the small model, and the human-in-the-loop checks that stop "debiasing" from turning into censorship. I'll also cover how we measured cost, latency and agreement with human reviewers before and after the switch.  **Key takeaways**  1. A practical path from prompt prototype to labelled dataset to an owned model 2. Designing and balancing a multi-label bias taxonomy 3. Where to keep humans in the loop, and how to measure fairness

Title: Stop Prompting Harder. Start Judging Better.
Abstract: Prompt tricks get you fluent answers. They do not tell you if the answer is the right thing to ship.  Teams burn cycles polishing system prompts, tool schemas, and RAG recipes while review queues grow and nobody owns the call when the model is wrong in a polite way. This talk is for people who build or lead LLM features and still have to live with the blast radius.  I will show a simple loop that sits on top of prompting: what changes the next action, what is noise, who verifies, and how you catch fluency without contact with reality. We will look at failure modes that prompting alone does not fix (confident wrongness, scope creep via agents, eval theater) and a lightweight way to design prompts, tools, and human review as one system.  You leave with a decision filter for AI output, a short checklist for prompt + eval + ownership, and language for pushing back on "just make the prompt better" when the real bottleneck moved. Cognition is cheap. Judgement is the craft.

Title: Observing AWS AgentCore with Datadog: End-to-End Observability for Autonomous AI
Abstract: AI agents are moving from experimental demos to production systems, reasoning over data, invoking tools, interacting with applications, and taking actions on behalf of the business. As these systems become more autonomous, traditional application monitoring alone is no longer enough. Engineers need visibility into not only whether an agent is running, but also what it is doing, which tools it is invoking, how models are behaving, and what each interaction costs.  This session presents a practical approach to end-to-end observability for autonomous AI using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Datadog. We will walk through a production-style AI agent running on AWS and trace a user request across the complete execution path — from agent orchestration and model interactions to tool invocations, downstream AWS services, infrastructure, and application telemetry.  Using Datadog APM, LLM Observability, Infrastructure Monitoring, Logs, and OpenTelemetry-compatible telemetry from AgentCore, we will demonstrate how AI-specific signals can be correlated with traditional application and infrastructure telemetry in a single operational view.  The session will show how observability can help engineers understand agent behavior, identify failed or unexpected tool calls, investigate latency and errors, detect abnormal token and cost consumption, and establish operational guardrails for production AI workloads.  Attendees will leave with a practical reference architecture and an SRE-oriented methodology for moving from simply deploying AI agents to operating autonomous AI reliably at production scale.

Title: Beyond Better Prompts: Designing Reliable Prompt Engineering Workflows for Production AI
Abstract: Prompt engineering is often presented as writing clever instructions for AI systems, but production environments introduce challenges that go far beyond prompt wording. Reliability, consistency, evaluation, security, context management, and workflow design become critical when AI systems move from experimentation into real applications.  In this session, I’ll explore prompt engineering from a practical systems perspective. We’ll discuss techniques for building reliable prompt workflows, structuring context, reducing inconsistent outputs, managing prompt evolution, and improving response quality through iterative design approaches.  The talk will also cover common mistakes teams make when deploying prompt-driven applications, including prompt drift, poor evaluation strategies, and over-reliance on manual experimentation.  Attendees will gain practical guidance on moving beyond isolated prompts and designing prompt engineering workflows that support scalable and maintainable AI applications.  Whether you're experimenting with generative AI or deploying LLM-powered systems in production, this session provides practical lessons and architectural insights that can be applied immediately.

Title: The Prompt Is Not the Policy: What Prompt Engineering Can and Can't Fix in Long-Horizon Agents
Abstract: Every agent team goes through the same arc. Something fails, you add a line to the prompt, it gets better. You do that forty times. Then you hit a class of failure where every prompt change fixes one case and breaks another, and no amount of rewriting moves the number. The useful question is how to recognise that boundary early instead of spending a quarter finding it.  I build computer-use agents — models that read screens, navigate real desktop and web software, and complete document and back-office workflows in regulated finance. This talk is about where the prompt stops being the right instrument, and what to do at that point.  The diagnostic first. Long-horizon failures split three ways: planning, visual grounding, and tool invocation. Prompting genuinely fixes a lot of grounding and tool-selection failures, and almost none of the planning ones — because planning failures are a credit-assignment problem thirty steps deep and the prompt has no way to reach back. I will show the failure-attribution setup that separates them, so you know which bucket you are in before you write another instruction.  Then the handoff. Your prompt iterations are not wasted when you move to post-training — they are labelled data. I will cover turning that history into trajectory-level preference pairs (preferring whole runs rather than single responses), where DPO and GRPO differ once episodes are long and expensive, and the specific trap of step-level preference data, which in our case produced more plausible-looking actions and fewer completed tasks.  And the honest ceiling: at 90% per-step reliability a thirty-step workflow completes 4% of the time. Prompting can raise per-step reliability. It cannot make the agent evaluate a plan before committing to it — that needs a model of the environment, which is the third act of the talk.  Takeaways: a test for whether your failure is prompt-fixable, a way to reuse prompt iterations as preference data, and a clear sense of the ceiling.

Title: You Cannot Fix a Prompt You Cannot See Fail: Debugging the Plan, Not Just the Answer
Abstract: Prompt engineering for single turn prompts has a tight feedback loop: change the prompt, read the output, judge it. Multi step and agentic prompting breaks that loop. When a reasoning chain goes wrong you see a bad final answer, but not which step chose the wrong path. You are tuning a plan you cannot see.  I authored the plan operation for agent planning spans in the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai#97), accepted upstream in May 2026. It makes the reasoning step a first class, portable span, so you can watch a prompting strategy plan, not just its final output. This talk shows how to instrument the planning step, how to tell a planning failure apart from a tool failure, and how to turn that signal into a measurement loop for prompt iteration. I will walk a demo, built for this talk, that catches a planning fault a final answer check would miss.

Title: Prompt Drift Kills: How to Make Prompts Stable
Abstract: Most prompt engineering guidance is intuition, but production teams need prompts that behave like software artifacts: versioned, testable, and resistant to drift. A small prompt edit or model change can break output structure, increase hallucinations, or blow up token budgets, and you only notice after users complain. This talk presents prompt contracts: a method that turns prompts into enforceable specifications using structured outputs, explicit invariants, and automated tests. We will define contract clauses such as required fields, banned claims, citation rules, and token ceilings, then enforce them with JSON schema validation plus a small suite of golden tests and fuzz tests. I will demo a real regression caused by a harmless prompt tweak, show how CI catches it, and fix it by tightening the contract and examples. The implementation uses Java for the application path and a lightweight Python harness for test execution, so teams can adopt it without changing their stack.

Title: Before You Rewrite the Prompt: Debug Agent Memory with SQL
Abstract: Your agent gives the wrong answer. You strengthen the prompt, add another example, and try again. But what if the relevant correction never reached the context window?  This talk separates three problems that often look like prompt failures: the right evidence was not stored, it was stored but not retrieved, or it was retrieved but ignored. We will use a small Python agent example and deliberately constructed stale-memory and retrieval-miss cases to show how to tell them apart.  The practical workflow records a run ID, memory candidates, selected context, tool calls, and the final answer. chDB lets us query those traces locally with SQL: which source version was used, which candidates were filtered out, and which runs regressed after a retrieval or prompt change? We then compare changes on a fixed question set, keeping retrieval quality separate from answer correctness.  Attendees will leave with a minimal trace schema, diagnostic queries, and an evaluation checklist for deciding when to change the prompt—and when to repair the data or retrieval pipeline instead. SQL makes evidence inspectable; it does not replace semantic evaluation, human review, or access controls.  For developers building RAG and agent applications. Basic Python and SQL familiarity is useful; no prior chDB experience is required.

Title: Personalizing RAG for Prompt-Driven Enterprise Analytics
Abstract: RAG can reduce hallucinated responses by over 60% compared with non-retrieval baselines, yet enterprise analytics systems often provide the same retrieval and response experience regardless of a user's expertise, role, or objective. This session explores how prompt-driven personalization can make enterprise RAG systems more useful for real-world analytics workflows.  The architecture combines three components: a User Profile Store, a Multi-Index Retrieval System, and a Personalized Generation Layer. Retrieval uses five specialized indices covering schemas, metric definitions, past queries, documentation, and curated SQL examples. Personalized re-ranking combines semantic similarity, user relevance, and recency, building on research reporting 10% to 31% improvements in mean average precision depending on query type.  The session demonstrates how retrieval context and generation behavior can adapt for three analyst personas. Senior data engineers can receive SQL-first responses, business analysts can receive narrative interpretations, and product managers can receive concise KPI-oriented summaries.  Drawing from production experience with a comparable system spanning SQL query history, dashboards, real-time analytics, and code notebooks at a billion-user-scale technology platform, the session also presents practical evaluation methods for retrieval personalization, response depth, format appropriateness, adaptation speed, and stale-profile detection.

Title: Beyond Basic RAG: Better Context for More Reliable Enterprise AI
Abstract: Prompt quality is only one part of building reliable AI systems. In enterprise environments, the quality of retrieved context, the freshness of knowledge, and the ability to govern information often have a greater impact on model responses than prompt wording alone. As Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) becomes the foundation for enterprise AI, designing effective retrieval pipelines has become essential for improving accuracy and consistency.  This session presents a practical five-axis framework for enterprise RAG systems covering ingestion, indexing, retrieval composition, grounding strategies, and governance. Based on a comparative study of approximately 25 academic, open source, and commercial implementations, including eight major enterprise platforms, the session examines how production systems differ from research prototypes and why capabilities such as ACL-aware retrieval, provenance tracking, and time-aware evaluation are increasingly important for trustworthy AI.  Attendees will also explore seven engineering challenges that continue to shape enterprise AI, including long-document grounding, retrieval across heterogeneous content, freshness through change data capture, confidentiality-preserving evaluation, multi-agent retrieval, and balancing latency with operational cost. Rather than focusing on prompt templates or a specific framework, the session provides a vendor-neutral perspective on designing knowledge systems that consistently deliver higher-quality context for enterprise AI applications.

Title: The Context Firewall: Securing AI Coding Assistants from Secrets and IP Leakage
Abstract: AI coding assistants are now deeply embedded in developer workflows, often given rich context source files, configs, logs, and even entire repositories: to generate useful code. But this creates a new security risk: developers can accidentally expose API keys, customer data, proprietary algorithms, or sensitive IP simply by asking for help. Traditional security controls don’t inspect what enters an LLM’s context window. The Context Firewall introduces a practical architecture to control what information AI assistants can send to external models. Instead of relying on developer awareness or provider settings, it enforces programmable controls across the AI-assisted development lifecycle. We’ll explore three layers of defense: Before the prompt: Classify and detect secrets, credentials, PII, and restricted files before they enter the model context. At the AI boundary: Inspect, redact, block, or transform sensitive context at an egress layer, based on organizational policy. Before the commit: Validate AI-generated code for exposed credentials, prohibited dependencies, or unsafe patterns before it reaches the repository. Using a practical example, we’ll demonstrate the flow: Developer → AI Assistant → Context Firewall → Policy Evaluation → Sanitized Context → LLM → Generated Code → Pre-Commit Validation But filtering prompts isn’t enough. Modern coding agents can read files, invoke tools, access terminals, and communicate with external services. Securing them requires treating context, tool permissions, and network egress as a single trust boundary.

Title: When Agents Decide: Accountability, Architecture and the Humans Left Holding the Liability
Abstract: Agentic AI is executing decisions faster than governance can follow. The accountability gaps it leaves behind are not hypothetical, and they were largely built in at the design stage.  The Case Agentic AI is no longer a research concept. It books travel, executes trades, screens job applicants, approves credit, and manages customer interactions, often with no human reviewing the individual decision before it is made. 2025 was the year the technology arrived. 2026 is the year organisations are discovering what they actually authorised.  The accountability problem is not subtle. When an agentic system causes harm, whether that is a discriminatory hiring decision, a wrongful credit refusal, or a safety-critical failure, the question of who is responsible is genuinely difficult to answer. The agent acted. No single human made the call. The decision may have emerged from a chain of micro-authorisations, none of which looked consequential at the time. Traditional liability frameworks were built on the assumption that a human made a decision and that a traceable chain of causation could be reconstructed. Agentic AI breaks both assumptions simultaneously.  The legal exposure is already crystallising. California AB 316, which took effect on 1 January 2026, explicitly forecloses the defence that an AI system's autonomous operation removes liability from the deployer. The EU's Product Liability Directive, due for implementation by December 2026, treats software including AI as a product subject to strict liability if found defective. Workday is currently facing a potential class action covering 1.1 billion job applications rejected by its AI screening tools. These are not regulatory abstractions. They are the downstream cost of governance decisions made, or not made, at the design and architecture stage.  Singapore's IMDA Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI, released at Davos in January 2026, introduced the concept of Meaningful Human Control, defined as the combination of human understanding, intervention capacity and traceability, precisely because existing frameworks were not designed for systems that can act, iterate and escalate permissions without human authorisation at each step. OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 identifies agent goal hijacking, identity and privilege abuse, and cascading failures as the most critical systemic risks. None of these are purely technology problems. They are governance problems that technical decisions either create or close.  This talk makes the case that the accountability gap in agentic AI sits partly with the engineers and architects who are making the scoping decisions that determine what the agent can touch, what it can escalate, and what it will never be asked to justify.  What Attendees Will Take Away A clear account of the current legal and regulatory landscape for agentic AI accountability, and specifically what it means for engineers and architects rather than compliance teams. A framework for auditing where accountability in their agentic systems is assumed rather than assigned. A practical understanding of the Meaningful Human Control concept and how to test whether it actually exists in a given system, or whether it has been designed out incrementally through a series of individually reasonable decisions. A set of questions to take back to their teams about permission architecture, escalation design, and the points at which human oversight breaks down.

Title: Why Single-Layer LLM Guardrails Fail: Lessons from Testing 390 Prompt Injection Attacks on AWS Bedrock
Abstract: Most teams protect their LLM applications with a single guardrail: a content filter, a system-prompt instruction, or one managed safety service. It looks fine in a demo. Then someone rephrases an attack, encodes it, or splits it across turns, and it gets through.  This talk shares what I learned building and testing guardrails for LLM and agentic AI systems on AWS Bedrock. I evaluated them against 390 attack prompts across 15 categories, including direct and indirect prompt injection, role-play jailbreaks, encoding and obfuscation tricks, and attempts to trigger destructive actions through an agent's tools.  We'll cover: - Why a single detection layer fails, and which attack categories get past it most easily - A dual-detection pattern that combines a managed guardrail with an independent second check, so each covers the other's blind spots - How to extend that into a layered architecture for AI agents, where catching a harmful action before it executes matters more than catching bad text - The tradeoff between false positives and false negatives, and why blocking too much is a real production failure too - An honest evaluation lesson: my first results file looked clean, but it turned out to contain only API throttling errors, not real model responses. How I caught it, and how to build an evaluation harness that won't fool you the same way.
